Title: OpenAI остается в Калифорнии и готовится к IPO, которое может стать одним из крупнейших в истории

Summary: 
OpenAI has reached an agreement with California's Attorney General Rob Bonta regarding its corporate restructuring, committing to remain in and expand within the state. This settlement removes a key obstacle to transforming the AI company into a more traditional commercial entity and paves the way for a potential initial public offering (IPO) in 2027, which could become one of the largest in history. The agreement follows months of legal scrutiny and political pressure, including threats from OpenAI to relocate if Bonta blocked the restructuring. CEO Sam Altman personally assured Bonta of his commitment to California, avoiding a legal battle or departure like Elon Musk's. Under the terms, OpenAI must stay in California and expand its presence. The new structure allows for an IPO, with the OpenAI Foundation (formerly the nonprofit parent) retaining control over the commercial entity and appointing its board of directors. The agreement includes a safety committee with authority to halt the release of new AI models, independent board oversight, and advance notice (at least three weeks) of significant structural or mission changes. The deal emerged amid intense political lobbying, with San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and influential Democratic lobbyists supporting OpenAI’s retention. Critics, including labor unions and nonprofit groups, had accused OpenAI of deviating from its original nonprofit mission. The company previously agreed to maintain nonprofit oversight in May. The restructuring shifts OpenAI’s 'limited-profit' model toward a conventional corporate structure, essential for IPO readiness and attracting more capital for AI development, while preserving oversight mechanisms to address concerns about mission creep.

Title: OpenAI may move forward with new business structure, partnership with Microsoft, regulators say

Summary: 
OpenAI has restructured its business model into a public benefit corporation, converting its for-profit arm under the control of its nonprofit board, with approval from Delaware and California attorneys general, who stated they would not oppose the plan. The move, finalized after nearly a year of negotiations, allows OpenAI to more easily monetize its AI technology while maintaining its nonprofit’s oversight. The company signed a revised agreement with Microsoft, granting the tech giant a 27% stake in the new for-profit entity, with updated terms on research access, commercial rights, and AGI (artificial general intelligence) verification. Under the new structure, AGI declarations will be verified by an independent expert panel, and Microsoft’s rights to confidential research and commercial use of products will extend until 2030 or 2032, whichever comes first. The nonprofit, now named the OpenAI Foundation, will distribute $25 billion toward health, disease cures, and AI cybersecurity, though the timeframe was not specified. The nonprofit retains control over board appointments and the power to halt product releases through its Safety and Security Committee. Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings emphasized the nonprofit’s authority, including the right to remove the for-profit board, while California’s Rob Bonta pledged continued oversight of OpenAI’s safety commitments. The restructuring follows the controversial removal and reappointment of CEO Sam Altman in November 2023. Despite regulatory approval, legal challenges persist: Elon Musk, a co-founder, continues to allege OpenAI betrayed its original mission, and a federal judge has declined to block the conversion but will expedite a trial on Musk’s claims. Robert Weissman of Public Citizen criticized the arrangement, arguing the nonprofit’s control is 'illusory' due to lack of demonstrated influence over the for-profit entity.

Summary: 
OpenAI has transitioned into a traditional for-profit company, marking a significant shift from its original mission as a nonprofit organization founded in 2015 to develop beneficial, ethical artificial general intelligence (AGI). The transformation, which culminated on October 28, 2025, involved restructuring into a capped-profit entity where the nonprofit foundation retains approximately 26%, Microsoft holds 27%, and employees and investors own the remaining 47%. Altman’s return in November 2023 coincided with the company’s decisive pivot toward commercialization. The reorganization faced resistance from former employees, AI safety experts, academic institutions, and public authorities—particularly the attorneys general of California and Delaware, who initially questioned the transfer of nonprofit assets and demanded legal safeguards. Musk even made a $97.4 billion acquisition offer in February 2025 to return OpenAI to open-source and safety-focused principles, which was rejected. The new agreement also solidifies OpenAI’s partnership with Microsoft, granting Microsoft guaranteed access to OpenAI’s models until 2023 while allowing both companies to develop their own AGI technologies. This marks a strategic consolidation of collaboration and competition.

Title: OpenAI完成重组 为IPO和人工智能投资铺平道路

Summary: 
In October 2025, OpenAI completed its corporate restructuring nearly a year after the turmoil caused by the abrupt ousting of CEO Sam Altman in late 2024. The restructuring, aimed at transforming OpenAI from a nonprofit into a for-profit entity to attract investors, faced strong opposition from Elon Musk, who sued to block it, claiming it violated the company’s founding principles. Musk also attempted but failed to acquire control of OpenAI’s nonprofit parent organization. Former employees and nonprofit leaders also urged regulators to intervene. Amid prolonged negotiations with Microsoft, OpenAI reached a new agreement and made concessions to Delaware’s Attorney General Kathy Jennings, who described the process as 'a long and tense negotiation.' Despite compromises, the restructuring marks a decisive victory, paving the way for massive investments in AI infrastructure—OpenAI has pledged $140 billion toward AI development. To fund this, OpenAI plans to raise capital through venture capital, debt financing, and ultimately an IPO, with Altman stating that an IPO remains the most likely path. SoftBank retains the right to withdraw its investment if the restructuring fails. OpenAI’s CFO Sarah Friar said the new structure will allow the company to 'raise funds in a simpler way.' However, concerns remain about the nonprofit’s actual influence over the for-profit entity: while the nonprofit board theoretically controls the for-profit board, in practice, all members except one serve on both boards, and the nonprofit lacks authority to fire the for-profit’s executives—highlighting a lack of independence. The nonprofit will hold 26% of the for-profit company’s equity (valued at $130 billion at a $500 billion valuation) and a warrant for additional shares if the company’s value grows more than 10-fold in 15 years. It plans to invest $2.5 billion in AI for healthcare and risk mitigation. Zico Kolter, the only nonprofit board member not on the for-profit board, chairs the Safety and Security Committee, which can delay product launches if safety standards are breached. The relationship with Microsoft remains complex: Microsoft will hold 27% of the new for-profit entity, but the terms of its ongoing access to OpenAI’s intellectual property—especially in areas like data centers and chip design—remain unclear. A new independent committee will determine when OpenAI reaches artificial general intelligence (AGI), at which point Microsoft will lose its 20% revenue share and access to OpenAI’s latest research. However, the committee’s composition, approval process, and evaluation criteria are still undefined. Elon Musk continues to oppose the restructuring, with his lawyer Marc Toberoff claiming the process ignored judicial recommendations for a jury trial, calling OpenAI’s complaints about reversal difficulties 'unfounded.'

The restructuring, aimed at transforming OpenAI from a nonprofit into a for-profit entity to attract investors, faced strong opposition from Elon Musk, who sued to block it, claiming it violated the company’s founding principles. Musk also attempted but failed to acquire control of OpenAI’s nonprofit parent organization. Former employees and nonprofit leaders also urged regulators to intervene. Amid prolonged negotiations with Microsoft, OpenAI reached a new agreement and made concessions to Delaware’s Attorney General Kathy Jennings, who described the process as 'a long and tense negotiation.' Despite compromises, the restructuring marks a decisive victory, paving the way for massive investments in AI infrastructure—OpenAI has pledged $140 billion toward AI development. To fund this, OpenAI plans to raise capital through venture capital, debt financing, and ultimately an IPO, with Altman stating that an IPO remains the most likely path. SoftBank retains the right to withdraw its investment if the restructuring fails. OpenAI’s CFO Sarah Friar said the new structure will allow the company to 'raise funds in a simpler way.' However, concerns remain about the nonprofit’s actual influence over the for-profit entity: while the nonprofit board theoretically controls the for-profit board, in practice, all members except one serve on both boards, and the nonprofit lacks authority to fire the for-profit’s executives—highlighting a lack of independence. The nonprofit will hold 26% of the for-profit company’s equity (valued at $130 billion at a $500 billion valuation) and a warrant for additional shares if the company’s value grows more than 10-fold in 15 years. It plans to invest $2.5 billion in AI for healthcare and risk mitigation. Zico Kolter, the only nonprofit board member not on the for-profit board, chairs the Safety and Security Committee, which can delay product launches if safety standards are breached. The relationship with Microsoft remains complex: Microsoft will hold 27% of the new for-profit entity, but the terms of its ongoing access to OpenAI’s intellectual property—especially in areas like data centers and chip design—remain unclear. A new independent committee will determine when OpenAI reaches artificial general intelligence (AGI), at which point Microsoft will lose its 20% revenue share and access to OpenAI’s latest research. However, the committee’s composition, approval process, and evaluation criteria are still undefined. Elon Musk continues to oppose the restructuring, with his lawyer Marc Toberoff claiming the process ignored judicial recommendations for a jury trial, calling OpenAI’s complaints about reversal difficulties 'unfounded.'
